Issued at 120 AM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Well, the day has arrived. Some people think it is the best holiday 
of the year, and in my opinion it is one of the best. A chance to be 
someone or something else, and of course, copious amounts of candy. 
The question is whether or not the weather will be spooky or if the 
weather will give us a trick or a treat on this last day of October 
and beyond. Well, you will find out in the discussion, that is why 
you are here after all. 

We still have the two weather systems that will impact the area over 
the next three days or so. The first is now moving northward through 
Utah and Colorado and will cross the area today, lifting northward 
into Montana by later this afternoon. This is the weaker of the two 
systems. Reasoning remains fairly similar to yesterday. It is that 
the most numerous showers will occur over western Wyoming (as high 
as a 4 out of 5 chance) with tapering chances further east. A shower 
can't be ruled out anywhere, but the smallest chance would be in 
Johnson and Natrona Counties where the chance is only 1 out of 10. 
The most numerous showers would occur through early afternoon, 
tapering off later in the afternoon with a lull expected to last 
most of the night. So, it looks like the weather has given us a 
treat when it comes to trick or treating earlier in the evening and 
for any adult gatherings later at night. The main chance of a shower 
this evening would again be in western Wyoming, but the chance 
is less than 1 out of 4, at least through midnight. As for 
amounts, the highest amounts would be focused in areas prone to 
southwest upslope flow, like the western Wind River Range. The 
chance of two tenths or greater would be confined to areas West 
of the Divide. Snow levels will remain above 8000 feet through 
this time as well, so impacts to travel would be minimal.

The main event still looks to be Sunday into Monday. The main 
players continue to be a long wave trough that will cross Wyoming 
Sunday night into Monday with associated upper level low that will 
pass into Colorado and then move northeast, inducing some lee 
cyclogenesis over Colorado. This will also phase with a stream of 
Pacific moisture as it moves into the Rockies. It still looks like 
the deepest moisture and heaviest precipitation will remain south of 
the area over Utah, Colorado and the desert Southwest, but most 
areas should see some precipitation from it. And, this will be a 
tale of two different upslope/downslope patterns. The steadiest
and heaviest precipitation on Sunday into Sunday evening will 
occur in western Wyoming and ares favored by west to 
northwesterly upslope, mainly to Tetons, Salt and Wyoming
Ranges, and the western Wind River Range. Then from later 
Sunday night into Monday, as the low passes to the east, the 
heaviest will shift East of the Divide to places favored by 
northerly upslope as moisture wraps around the developing low. 
This favors places like from south of Riverton to Lander and 
eastward to Casper, the southern Bighorn Basin from Thermopolis 
to south of Worland, as well as the Cody Foothills and the Bighorn
Range. With the north flow, places like the eastern Bighorn 
Basin, northern Wind River Basin, and much of the Green River 
Basin would see the least with downsloping flow.

Then there are two more questions, how much total precipitation and 
potential snow and how much could fall. We will start with 
precipitation. Most areas, except the southern Green River 
Basin, have at least a 1 in 2 chance of a quarter of an inch or
QPF between 6 am Sunday and 6 am Tuesday. The aforementioned 
favored areas that were mentioned above are the areas what have 
at least a 1 in 2 chance of over three quarters of an inch of 
QPF in that same timeframe. The greater than 1 in 2 chance of 
inch or more is largely restricted to the highest elevations 
though. Precipitation should taper off by sunset Monday, with 
all areas dry by Tuesday morning.

Now for the more juicy or should I say, cooler question - what 
about snow? The air with this system is of Pacific origin, and 
as a result not the coldest in the world. The coolest 700 
millibar temperatures look to drop to is minus 4, which would 
keep snow levels at roughly 6500 feet or higher. So, most 
population centers and roads outside of the mountain passes 
would see mainly rain or only wet snow that would not cause many
problems. Most locations above 7500 feet should see some 
accumulation though. As for advisory amounts of snow (6 to 12 
inches of snow in the mountains), the chance of this is largely 
above 8500 feet. However, this does include Teton and Togwotee 
Passes in western Wyoming as well as Granite and Powder River 
Passes in the Bighorn Range. We will likely (a greater than 3 
out of 5 chance) have some advisories in the mountain ranges. 
However, with main impact Sunday afternoon to Monday morning, we
